alignment.note: The Vulgate omits the entire opening clause 'And having sat down' (Καὶ καθίσας / ܘܝܬܒ), proceeding directly to the action with the child. This represents a substantive textual divergence in narrative sequence.

The Peshitta explicitly names Jesus (ܝܫܘܥ) as the subject, a typical Syriac clarification where Greek relies on participial construction and context. Neither Greek nor Latin include the proper name here.

The Vulgate omits 'he called the Twelve' (ἐφώνησεν τοὺς δώδεκα / ܘܩܪܐ ܠܬܪܥܣܪ) entirely, replacing the entire narrative action with a scene involving a child (accipiens puerum). This represents a major textual variant, likely reflecting confusion with Mark 9:36.

The Vulgate inserts 'Et accipiens puerum, statuit eum in medio eorum : quem cum complexus esset' (taking a child, setting him in their midst, embracing him), harmonising with Mark 9:36. This material appears nowhere in the Greek or Peshitta witnesses for this verse.

Greek uses coordinating conjunction καὶ with present tense λέγει; Peshitta employs simple ܘܐܡܪ ܠܗܘܢ; Vulgate uses relative pronoun + temporal clause 'quem cum complexus esset, ait illis'. All convey speech introduction but with different syntactic frames.

The Vulgate completely omits the conditional protasis 'If anyone desires to be first' (εἴ τις θέλει πρῶτος εἶναι / ܡܢ ܕܨܒܐ ܕܢܗܘܐ ܩܕܡܝܐ), proceeding directly to teaching content. This constitutes a major textual divergence in the logical structure of Jesus' saying.

Greek uses future ἔσται with genitive πάντων ἔσχατος ('he will be last of all'); Peshitta employs jussive ܢܗܘܐ ܐܚܪܝܐ ܕܟܠ ܐܢܫ ('let him be last of every man'), adding the explicit noun ܐܢܫ. The Vulgate omits this clause entirely, representing a major textual variant.

The Vulgate omits the second half of the saying 'and servant of all' (καὶ πάντων διάκονος / ܘܡܫܡܫܢܐ ܕܟܠ ܐܢܫ). The Peshitta again adds ܐܢܫ ('man') after ܕܟܠ, making explicit what Greek leaves as genitive plural πάντων.
